chapters.n: The book of Helaman opens around 52 BC with trouble. The peace that ended Alma’s record quickly gives way to a political crisis among the Nephites.

f.g: Counting from the start of the reign of the judges, about 91 BC; so roughly 52 BC.

chapters.n: Pahoran, the loyal chief judge who had worked with Captain Moroni, has died. His sons now argue over who should take his place in the judgment-seat.

f.w: gone the way of all the earth
f.g: A traditional way of saying someone died.

chapters.n: Three brothers compete for the office, and their rivalry spreads to the people, who take sides.
Pahoran had many sons, but only these three sought the office. The result is three factions splitting the nation.
The people vote, and the younger Pahoran, son of the former chief judge, is chosen. The Nephite system relied on “the voice of the people.”
Pacumeni accepts the result gracefully and joins the majority, a model of how to lose an election well.
Paanchi and his supporters are furious. He begins to use flattery to stir them toward armed rebellion.

f.g: Angry.

chapters.n: Before he can act, Paanchi is arrested, tried by the people’s law, and condemned to death for trying to overturn their liberty.
Paanchi’s angry followers hire a man named Kishkumen, who murders the new chief judge Pahoran right on the judgment-seat. Political murder enters Nephite history here.
Pahoran’s servants chase the assassin, but he escapes too quickly to be caught.
The conspirators bind themselves with an oath, sworn by God their Maker, never to reveal the murderer. This secret oath is the seed of the Gadianton robbers.

f.g: God, the eternal Creator; they misuse His name to seal a wicked pact.

chapters.n: Because Kishkumen was disguised, no one knew who he was. His band blended into society; those who were discovered were executed, but many remained hidden.
Pacumeni, next in line, is appointed chief judge by the people, as was his right. The crisis of the fortieth year seems to be over.
The next year (about 51 BC), the Lamanites raise a huge, heavily armed army. The internal turmoil has left the Nephites vulnerable.

f.g: Scimitars; curved swords or cutting weapons.
Helmets or head protection.

chapters.n: Their leader is Coriantumr, a Nephite dissenter descended from Zarahemla (the Mulekite founder of the city), a big, powerful man.

f.g: Not the Jaredite king of the same name in Omni 1:21 and Ether.

chapters.n: Tubaloth, the Lamanite king and son of Ammoron, believes Coriantumr’s strength and cunning can finally beat the Nephites.
So Tubaloth stirs up his people’s anger, gathers his armies, and sends them under Coriantumr straight toward Zarahemla.
Distracted by political strife, the Nephites had not kept enough guards in the capital. They assumed no enemy would dare strike the heart of the land.

f.g: Would not dare.

chapters.n: Coriantumr marches so fast that the Nephites have no time to assemble an army.
He kills the guards at the city gate, pours in with his whole army, and takes all of Zarahemla.

f.g: The guards posted at the entrance.

chapters.n: Pacumeni, the chief judge, flees to the city wall, where Coriantumr kills him. Two chief judges have now died violently in two years.
Holding the strongest city in the land, Coriantumr grows bold and plans to conquer the whole country.

f.g: Stronghold; best-defended place.

chapters.n: Instead of staying put, he marches north toward Bountiful, intending to cut his way through and seize the northern lands.
Thinking the Nephites’ main strength lay in the center, he pushes fast, catching them only in small groups and cutting them down.
Yet this bold drive into the center of the land actually gives Moronihah, the Nephite commander, a great advantage, despite heavy Nephite losses.
Moronihah had stationed his strongest forces on the borders, expecting the Lamanites to attack outlying cities as before. He had not expected a strike at the center.

f.g: Until now.

chapters.n: The Lamanites proved bolder than Moronihah hoped. They took the capital and slaughtered men, women, and children while seizing many cities.
Once he learns what happened, Moronihah sends Lehi with an army around to cut off the Lamanites before they reach Bountiful.

f.g: Get ahead of them; intercept them.

chapters.n: Lehi intercepts them and attacks, forcing them to retreat back toward Zarahemla.
Moronihah meets them on their retreat. In a very bloody battle, Coriantumr himself is killed.
The Lamanites are completely surrounded, with no escape in any direction.
Coriantumr’s daring plan has trapped his own army deep in Nephite territory. With their leader dead, the Lamanites surrender.
Moronihah retakes Zarahemla and, in a merciful act, lets the Lamanite prisoners go home in peace.

f.w: depart out of the land in peace

chapters.n: So ends the forty-first year of the judges (about 51 BC). The capital is restored, but the hidden band that murdered Pahoran is still at large.
About 50 BC, with peace restored by Moronihah, the judgment-seat sits empty after Pacumeni’s death. Once more people argue over who should fill it.

f.w: no one to fill the judgment-seat

chapters.n: The people choose Helaman, son of the Helaman who led the stripling warriors. He is also the keeper of the sacred records, so this book bears his name.

f.w: Helaman, who was the son of Helaman

chapters.n: Kishkumen, Pahoran’s secret murderer, now plans to kill Helaman too, protected by his band’s oath of silence.
Enter Gadianton, a smooth talker skilled in the “craft” of secret murder and robbery. He takes over Kishkumen’s band, which will soon bear his name.

f.g: Skill or cunning, here used for wicked ends.

chapters.n: Gadianton wins them with flattery: put him in the judgment-seat and he will give his followers power and office. Their goal is not justice but control.
As Kishkumen heads to murder Helaman, one of Helaman’s servants, who had gone out in disguise at night, has already discovered the band’s plans.

f.g: The servant apparently posed as one of the conspirators to learn their secrets.

chapters.n: The servant meets Kishkumen and gives him the band’s secret sign. Thinking he is a fellow member, Kishkumen reveals his plan and asks for help reaching Helaman.

f.g: A secret signal used by members of the band to recognize one another.

chapters.n: Now the servant understands the whole conspiracy: murder, robbery, and seizing power. Mormon calls it their “combination,” a word he will use for organized evil throughout the book.

f.g: A secret alliance or conspiracy.

chapters.n: On the way, the servant kills Kishkumen with a single stab to the heart, then runs to tell Helaman everything. The would-be assassin is stopped by his own secret methods.

f.g: Instantly, without making a sound.

chapters.n: Helaman sends officers to arrest the band so they can be tried and punished under the law.
When Kishkumen does not return, Gadianton fears discovery and leads his band out of the land by a secret route into the wilderness. When the officers arrive, they are gone.
Mormon promises more about Gadianton later. The forty-second year of the judges ends (about 50 BC).
A sobering prophecy: this Gadianton and what he started will bring about the downfall, almost the complete destruction, of the Nephite people.
Mormon clarifies that he means the end of the whole record of Nephi he is abridging (the large plates), not the end of the book of Helaman.

f.g: Mormon’s source, the large plates of Nephi, covering Nephite history to his own day.

chapters.n: In the forty-third year (about 49 BC) there was little conflict, only a bit of pride in the church that caused minor disagreements, and those were resolved by year’s end.
Two more years pass with little or no strife. Mormon keeps careful track of years of peace as well as years of trouble.
In the forty-sixth year contention returns, and a great many people leave Zarahemla to settle in the land northward.
They travel very far, reaching large bodies of water and many rivers.
They spread into every part of the land that had not been stripped of trees by earlier inhabitants.

f.g: Made bare or empty.

chapters.n: The land wasn’t empty of good soil, only of timber. It was called “desolate” because an earlier people, the Jaredites, had been destroyed there.
With little wood available, the settlers became experts in cement and built their houses of it. Ancient Mesoamerica did make wide use of lime-based cement and plaster.

f.g: A hardened building material, likely lime-based plaster or concrete.

chapters.n: The Nephites grow and spread so widely that they seem to fill the land from sea to sea.

f.w: from the sea south to the sea north

chapters.n: They lived in tents and cement houses and deliberately let new trees grow so they could build later. It’s an early example of careful land stewardship.

f.g: Allow.
Places of assembly for worship and teaching.

chapters.n: Because timber was so scarce in the north, much of it was shipped in.
With imported wood and their own cement, the northern settlers built many cities.
Many of the people of Ammon, Lamanite converts by birth, also moved north.
Mormon pauses: this people kept many detailed and lengthy records about themselves.
He admits that he cannot include even a hundredth of the history: wars, preaching, ship-building, temple-building, righteousness and wickedness. What we have is a careful selection.
The records come in many kinds of books, kept mostly by the Nephites.
Mormon looks ahead to his own time, when the Nephites would fall into sin, be destroyed or scattered, and mix with the Lamanites until the name “Nephite” disappeared.
Returning to his story, Mormon notes that the migrations he just described happened after a period of great contention and war.
The forty-sixth year ends.
Contention continues through the forty-seventh and forty-eighth years.
Through it all, Helaman governs with justice and fairness, keeping God’s laws and following his father’s example, and he prospers.

f.g: Fairness; impartial justice.

f.w: walk after the ways of his father

chapters.n: Helaman names his sons Nephi and Lehi after their great ancestors. These two will become powerful prophets later in the book.
Late in the forty-eighth year, the wars and strife begin to ease a little.
In the forty-ninth year there is lasting peace, except that Gadianton’s secret combination has quietly rooted itself in the populated areas. Leaders don’t know about it, so it survives.
That same year the church flourishes, with thousands baptized “unto repentance.”
The growth and blessings are so great that even the church’s leaders are amazed.
Tens of thousands join the church. It is one of the largest periods of conversion in Nephite history.
Mormon draws a lesson with his signature phrase “thus we may see”: the Lord is merciful to everyone who sincerely calls on Him.

f.g: Mormon’s usual signal that he is pausing to teach a lesson from the history.

chapters.n: Heaven’s gate is open to all who believe in Jesus Christ, the Son of God. No one is shut out by birth or background.

f.w: the gate of heaven is open unto all

chapters.n: God’s word is “quick” (alive) and powerful. It cuts through the devil’s traps and guides the follower of Christ along a narrow path over a gulf of misery, like the iron rod in Lehi’s dream.
Holding to God’s word brings the soul safely to God’s right hand, to sit with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and the faithful, never to leave His presence again.

f.w: sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and with Jacob

chapters.n: That year there was constant rejoicing throughout all Nephite lands.
Peace and great joy continue through the rest of the forty-ninth year and the fiftieth year.
In the fifty-first year pride creeps in, not into the church as God’s institution, but into the hearts of people who claimed membership in it. Mormon carefully separates the two.

f.g: Claimed or declared.

chapters.n: These proud members persecute their humbler brothers and sisters. Mormon calls this a great evil.
Yet the humble respond by fasting and praying, growing firmer in faith and full of joy. Their hearts are sanctified, made pure and holy, because they yield their hearts to God.
The fifty-second year ends in peace, except for growing pride caused by great wealth, a danger that increases day by day.
In the fifty-third year (about 39 BC), Helaman dies. His eldest son Nephi becomes chief judge and, like his father, rules justly and keeps God’s commandments.
Around 38 BC the pride noted earlier boils over. Dissension in the church and contention among the people lead to actual bloodshed.
The rebels are defeated and expelled, and they go over to the Lamanite king, a pattern repeated again and again in the Book of Mormon.
They try to stir the Lamanites to war, but the Lamanites, remembering past defeats, are too afraid to listen at first.
Two years later more Nephite dissenters arrive and, together with the first group, succeed in rousing the Lamanites. They spend the whole year preparing for war.
The invasion comes, and by the fifty-eighth year (about 34 BC) the Lamanites hold Zarahemla and all the land as far as Bountiful.

f.g: A grim phrase for war and killing.

chapters.n: The Nephites and Moronihah’s armies are pushed all the way back to Bountiful.
There they build a defensive line across the land from west sea to east sea, about a day’s journey long, to protect the north.

f.w: a day's journey for a Nephite

chapters.n: Through Nephite traitors and a huge Lamanite army, all Nephite lands in the south are lost within two years.
In the sixtieth year Moronihah begins winning back cities that had fallen.
By the sixty-first year they have regained half of everything they lost.
Mormon explains why: the loss would never have happened without their wickedness, including among people who claimed to be church members.

f.w: professed to belong to the church

chapters.n: Mormon lists their sins: pride from wealth, oppressing the poor, refusing food and clothing to the needy, abusing the humble, mocking sacred things, rejecting revelation, and violence, dishonesty, and immorality. Neglect of the poor stands at the head.

f.w: withholding their food from the hungry
smiting their humble brethren upon the cheek
f.g: Striking on the cheek was an insult as well as an injury.

chapters.n: Because they boasted in their own strength, God left them to their own strength, and it failed. Without God’s help, they were driven back until they lost nearly everything.
Moronihah, along with Nephi and Lehi, the sons of Helaman, preached repentance and warned what would happen if the people did not change.
The people repented, and as they did, they began to prosper again. The connection is direct.
Seeing their repentance, Moronihah dared to lead them on the offensive, and they regained half of their property and lands.
The sixty-first year of the judges ends.
In the sixty-second year Moronihah can gain no more ground.
The Lamanites are simply too many, so the Nephites give up trying to reclaim the rest and focus on holding what they have.

f.g: Plan or intention.

chapters.n: Facing such numbers, the Nephites fear they will be overrun and destroyed.
Fear brings memory. They recall the warnings of Alma and King Mosiah and admit they had been stubborn and had ignored God’s commandments.

f.g: Stubborn, like an animal that won’t bend its neck to the yoke.

chapters.n: They realize they had corrupted the laws Mosiah gave by the Lord’s direction, and that they had become as wicked as the Lamanites they once looked down on.
The church dwindled, faith in prophecy and revelation faded, and they could see God’s judgments coming.

f.w: the judgments of God did stare them in the face
f.g: God’s consequences were plainly in view, impossible to ignore.

chapters.n: The Spirit no longer protected them, because the Spirit of the Lord does not dwell in unholy temples. Here “temples” means people’s own bodies and lives.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord doth not dwell in unholy temples

chapters.n: God stopped preserving them by miracles because of their unbelief. Outnumbered, they now see they must hold fast to the Lord or perish.

f.g: Unequaled; without match.
Hold tightly to; stay close to.

chapters.n: Man for man, they were no stronger than the Lamanites. Their former edge had come from God, and sin had taken it away in just a few years.

f.w: in the space of not many years

chapters.n: That same year (about 30 BC), Nephi gives up his office as chief judge to a man named Cezoram.

Mormon explains why: Nephite government rested on the voice of the people, and now most people were choosing evil. Their laws had become corrupt, so the society was “ripening” for destruction, as Mosiah had warned.

f.w: they who chose evil were more numerous than they who chose good

f.g: Growing steadily toward judgment, like fruit ripening for harvest.

chapters.n: The people were so stubborn that law and justice could no longer restrain them; only destruction would.

f.g: Stubborn and unwilling to submit.

chapters.n: Weary of their wickedness, Nephi steps down to preach for the rest of his life, and his brother Lehi joins him. Like Alma before him, he sees preaching as a stronger remedy than government.
They are moved by remembering their father Helaman’s counsel, which Mormon now quotes.
Helaman explains why he named his sons Nephi and Lehi: so that remembering their own names would remind them of their ancestors, whose works were good. A name can be a call to live up to something.

f.w: the names of our first parents

f.g: A key word in the Book of Mormon; to remember is to keep in mind and act on.

chapters.n: He wants his sons to do good so that, like their namesakes, people will say and write good things about them.
But motive matters. They should not do good to be praised, but to lay up lasting treasure in heaven and receive eternal life, as their fathers did.
“Remember, remember” is repeated for emphasis. Helaman reminds them of King Benjamin’s teaching: salvation comes only through the atoning blood of Jesus Christ, who would come to redeem the world.
He also recalls Amulek’s words to Zeezrom: Christ comes to save people from their sins, not in their sins. He frees us from sin rather than excusing us while we stay in it.

f.w: not come to redeem them in their sins

chapters.n: The Father gave Christ power to redeem people on condition of repentance. Angels have announced these “conditions of repentance,” which open the way to the Redeemer’s saving power.
One of the best-loved verses in the Book of Mormon. Build your life on Christ, the rock. The devil’s storms will still come, but they cannot drag you down, because that foundation never fails.

f.g: Arrows or spears; here, the devil’s attacks.

chapters.n: Mormon notes that Helaman taught his sons much more than is recorded here, both written and unwritten.
The brothers act on their father’s words. They begin a preaching mission among the Nephites, starting at the city of Bountiful.
From Bountiful they go to Gid, then to Mulek, cities on the eastern coast that had been battlegrounds in Captain Moroni’s day.
They visit every Nephite city in the land southward, then go into Zarahemla itself, which was now under Lamanite control.

f.w: the land of Zarahemla, among the Lamanites

chapters.n: Their preaching is so powerful that many Nephite dissenters confess, are baptized, and go back to the Nephites to make amends for the harm they had done. True repentance includes making things right.
Nephi and Lehi have authority from God to preach, and God even gives them the words to say.

f.w: what they should speak given unto them

chapters.n: The Lamanites are astonished and convinced. Eight thousand in and around Zarahemla are baptized and turn away from the false traditions they had been taught.
The brothers then travel deep into Lamanite territory, to the land of Nephi.
A Lamanite army captures them and throws them into the same prison where King Limhi once held Ammon and his companions.
After many days without food, their captors come to take them out and kill them.
Suddenly Nephi and Lehi are surrounded by what looks like fire. The guards are afraid to touch them, yet the brothers are not burned.
Seeing that the pillar of fire protects rather than harms them, the brothers take courage.
Their captors stand frozen, too amazed to move or come near.

f.g: Unable to speak.

chapters.n: Nephi and Lehi reassure them: God is showing them this wonder to prove they cannot kill His servants.
The earth quakes and the prison walls shake violently but do not fall. The crowd in the prison is made up of Lamanites and Nephite dissenters.
A cloud of darkness covers them, and an awful, solemn fear falls on them. The darkness mirrors their spiritual state.
A voice from above the darkness calls them to repent and to stop trying to kill the servants God sent with good news.

f.g: Good news; the gospel.

chapters.n: The voice is not thunder or noise. It is still and perfectly mild, like a whisper, yet it pierces to the soul. God’s most powerful messages often come quietly.

f.w: a still voice of perfect mildness

chapters.n: Gentle as it is, the voice shakes the earth and the walls, and the darkness remains.
The voice speaks a second time, adding that “the kingdom of heaven is at hand,” the same message later preached by John the Baptist and Jesus.

f.w: the kingdom of heaven is at hand

chapters.n: A third time the voice speaks marvelous words too sacred to be written. Threefold divine messages appear elsewhere, as when the Father speaks three times before Christ appears in Bountiful.
Trapped by the darkness and frozen by fear, the Lamanites cannot run.
One man in the crowd was a Nephite by birth who had once belonged to the church but had left it.
Turning around, he sees through the darkness that Nephi’s and Lehi’s faces are shining like angels’. They are looking upward, as if speaking with someone they can see.
He calls the others to look, and they are given power to turn and see the shining faces too.
They ask what this means and who the brothers are talking with.
The man, Aminadab, tells them Nephi and Lehi are speaking with angels of God. His earlier church experience lets him recognize what is happening.

f.g: Mentioned only here; a former church member whose old faith revives in this moment.

chapters.n: The crowd asks the most important question: what must we do to remove this darkness?
Aminadab answers: repent and cry out to the voice until you have faith in Christ, as taught by Alma, Amulek, and Zeezrom. Then the darkness will lift.
They all cry out to the One who shook the earth, and they keep praying until the darkness is gone.
When they look around, every one of them is now encircled by the same pillar of fire that protected Nephi and Lehi.
The fire does not harm them or the prison walls. They are filled with joy too great for words and full of glory.

f.w: joy which is unspeakable and full of glory

chapters.n: The Holy Ghost enters their hearts like fire, and they speak marvelous words. The outward fire becomes an inward one, which Latter-day Saints recognize as the baptism of fire.
Another pleasant, whispering voice speaks to them.
The voice is the Father’s, bringing peace because of their faith in His “Well Beloved,” Jesus Christ, chosen from before the world was created.

f.w: from the foundation of the world

chapters.n: Looking up, they see the heavens open and angels come down to minister to them.
About 300 people witness all this. They are told to go out, not to marvel or doubt.

f.g: These witnesses become missionaries to their own people.

chapters.n: They share what they saw and heard everywhere, and because the evidence is so strong, most of the Lamanites are convinced.
Those converted lay down their weapons, their hatred, and their inherited traditions. Conversion changes both behavior and the heart.

f.w: lay down their weapons of war

chapters.n: They even give back to the Nephites the lands they had conquered, an extraordinary peace offering.
A surprising reversal: by about 29 BC most Lamanites have become a righteous people, even more faithful than the Nephites, because they stayed firm and steady in their new faith.

f.w: firmness and their steadiness in the faith

chapters.n: Many Nephites, by contrast, had become hard-hearted, unrepentant, and openly wicked, rejecting all the preaching and prophecy they heard.

f.g: Unwilling to repent.

chapters.n: Still, faithful church members rejoice at the Lamanites’ conversion and enjoy warm fellowship with their new brothers and sisters.

f.g: Friendship and shared life as fellow believers.

chapters.n: Lamanite converts come to Zarahemla to tell the Nephites how they were converted and to urge them to believe and repent. The former “enemies” now become missionaries to the Nephites.
Many of these Lamanites preach with great power, bringing many Nephites to deep humility as followers of God and “the Lamb,” a title for Christ.
Lamanite preachers, along with Nephi and Lehi, go north to preach. The sixty-third year ends.
Peace is so complete that Nephites can travel anywhere, even through Lamanite lands.
Lamanites can travel freely too, and the two peoples trade openly. “Free intercourse” here means open travel and commerce.

f.g: Free interaction and trade between peoples.

chapters.n: Peace and open trade bring great wealth to both peoples, with abundant gold, silver, and other precious metals.
Mormon explains place names: the southern land was called Lehi and the northern land Mulek, after the son of King Zedekiah whom the Lord brought to the northern land.
Both lands are rich in ores, and skilled metalworkers refine them.

f.g: Skilled craftsmen.

chapters.n: Agriculture thrives too: abundant grain, growing population, and many flocks and herds.

f.g: Young animals fattened for food.

chapters.n: Women spin and weave fine cloth of all kinds. The sixty-fourth year passes in peace.

f.g: High-quality cloth woven from finely twisted thread.

chapters.n: The sixty-fifth year also brings joy, peace, and much preaching and prophecy about Christ’s coming.
Then a shock: the chief judge Cezoram is murdered by an unknown assassin on the judgment-seat, and soon his son, chosen to replace him, is murdered too.
From the start of the sixty-seventh year the people quickly turn wicked again.
The cause: long prosperity. Without war to unite them, they set their hearts on riches and want to rise above one another, which leads to secret murder, robbery, and plunder.
The murderers are Gadianton’s band, founded by Kishkumen and Gadianton. They have grown among the Nephites but are even more numerous among the wickeder Lamanites.
This band killed Cezoram and his son, and no one could find the killers.
When the Lamanites discover the robbers among them, they are grieved and use every means to wipe them out.
But most Nephites, stirred up by Satan, join the bands instead, swearing oaths to protect each other from punishment for murder and theft.
Members used secret signs and passwords to recognize each other, so no member would ever be harmed by another, whatever crime he committed.
These oaths let them commit every kind of crime and immorality against both the laws of their country and the laws of God.

f.g: Sexual immorality.

chapters.n: Any member who exposed the band was judged not by the nation’s laws but by the band’s own wicked laws from Gadianton and Kishkumen, meaning punishment by death.
These are the very oaths and covenants Alma told his son Helaman to keep hidden, so that they would not lead people to destruction.

f.w: Alma commanded his son should not go forth

chapters.n: Gadianton did not learn the oaths from the sacred records. Satan, the same being who tempted Adam and Eve in Eden, put them into his heart.
The same being plotted with Cain, promising that his murder of Abel would stay secret, and has worked with Cain’s followers ever since. The Book of Moses tells this story in detail.
Satan also inspired the Tower of Babel and led the Jaredites, who came from that tower, into the same secret works until they were utterly destroyed.
The same tempter inspires Gadianton to keep up secret murder. These works have existed since the beginning of mankind.
Satan is the author of all sin. He passes down his plots and oaths from generation to generation wherever he can win people’s hearts.
He has gained a strong grip on the Nephites. Most have abandoned righteousness and made idols of their gold and silver, worshiping wealth itself.

f.w: idols of their gold and their silver

chapters.n: All this happens within just a few years, mostly in the sixty-seventh year. Spiritual decline can be swift.

f.w: in the space of not many years

chapters.n: Wickedness keeps growing in the sixty-eighth year, to the grief of the righteous.

f.g: Mourning; expressions of grief.

chapters.n: Mormon’s “thus we see”: the Nephites dwindle in unbelief while the Lamanites grow in knowledge of God and live truthfully and uprightly.
The Spirit begins to withdraw from the Nephites because their hearts are wicked and hard.

f.w: the Spirit of the Lord began to withdraw

chapters.n: Meanwhile, the Lord pours out His Spirit on the Lamanites because they are willing and quick to believe. Openness to God’s word, not ancestry, invites the Spirit.
The Lamanites hunt down the Gadianton band and preach to its members, until the robbers are completely wiped out among the Lamanites. Preaching, not only force, ends the problem.
The Nephites do the opposite. They support the robbers until the bands spread through all their lands and even lure many righteous people into sharing their spoils and crimes.

f.g: Led astray; enticed into wrongdoing.

chapters.n: The robbers gain sole control of the government and use it to crush and ignore the poor, the meek, and the humble followers of God.
Mormon concludes that the Nephites are in a terrible state, ripening for everlasting destruction.
The sixty-eighth year of the judges ends, about 24 BC.
About 23 BC, Nephi, son of Helaman, comes back to Zarahemla after a mission in the land northward.
He had preached and prophesied there among the northern settlers.
They rejected everything he taught, so he could not stay and returned to his homeland.

f.g: Birth; “the land of his nativity” means his native land.

chapters.n: Home is no better. Gadianton robbers now sit in the judgment-seats, having seized power illegally. They ignore God’s commandments and give no justice to anyone.

f.g: Took power wrongfully, without legal right.

chapters.n: These corrupt judges condemn the innocent, free the guilty for bribes, and hold office only to gain wealth and fame and to sin more easily. Justice has been turned upside down.

f.w: letting the guilty and the wicked go unpunished because of their money

chapters.n: This collapse happened in only a few years. Seeing it, Nephi’s heart swells with sorrow, and he cries out in anguish.

f.w: in the space of not many years

chapters.n: Nephi wishes he had lived in the days of his ancestor Nephi, when the people were easy to persuade, firm in obedience, slow to sin, and quick to listen to the Lord.

f.g: His forefather Nephi, son of Lehi; “father” often means ancestor in scripture.
Willing to listen and be persuaded.

chapters.n: If he had lived then, he says, he could have rejoiced in his people’s righteousness.
But he accepts that these are his days, a time when his soul will be sorrowful. Like many prophets, he serves in the age he is given.

f.g: Resigned to; accepting that this is his lot.

chapters.n: Mormon sets the scene: Nephi was praying on a tower in his garden, beside the main road to Zarahemla’s central market, near the garden gate. It was a very public spot.

f.g: Probably a raised platform or small structure used for prayer and rest, not a military tower.

chapters.n: Passers-by see Nephi pouring out his soul to God and spread the word. Crowds gather to find out why he is mourning over the people’s wickedness.
When Nephi finishes praying and stands up, he sees a large crowd assembled.
Nephi turns to them: Why have you come? So I can tell you about your sins?
He explains that he climbed his tower simply to pour out his grief to God, grief caused by their wickedness.
They marvel at his mourning, but he tells them what they should really marvel at: how firmly the devil has gripped their hearts.

f.g: Given over; surrendered.

chapters.n: How could they give in to the one who wants to hurl their souls into endless misery?
Nephi pleads: repent, turn to the Lord. Why choose death? His words echo Ezekiel’s plea to Israel.
The Lord has not abandoned them without reason. They hardened their hearts and refused to hear the Good Shepherd, Jesus Christ, and so provoked His anger.
Instead of gathering them like a shepherd, the Lord will scatter them unless they repent, leaving them prey to dogs and wild beasts.

f.w: meat for dogs and wild beasts

chapters.n: How could they forget God so soon after He rescued them? Their recent deliverance from the Lamanites through Nephi and Lehi’s preaching was fresh.
Nephi names their motives: gain, praise, gold and silver. Their hearts are set on vain riches, and for them they murder, steal, and lie.
Unless they repent, Zarahemla and the surrounding cities will be taken from them, because the Lord will no longer give them strength against their enemies.

f.w: will not grant unto you strength

chapters.n: The Lord’s rule: He shows His protecting strength only to those who repent and listen. Unless they repent, the Lamanites will fare better than the Nephites.

f.g: A prophet’s formula for delivering God’s own words.

chapters.n: The Lamanites are more righteous because they have not sinned against great knowledge. Those who know more are held more accountable, so the Lord will be merciful to the Lamanites.
A first “wo”: they have joined Gadianton’s secret band, a great abomination.

f.g: An old spelling of “woe”: sorrow or disaster to come.

chapters.n: A second “wo”: they let pride, fed by their great wealth, lift them up beyond what is good.
A third “wo” for all their wickedness. The repeated “wo” pattern recalls the prophets of Israel and Jacob.
Unless they repent, they will perish, lose their lands, and be wiped from the earth.
Nephi stresses that this warning is not his own idea. God has revealed it to him, so he testifies it will surely happen.

f.w: not of myself that I know these things

chapters.n: Some judges in the crowd, secret members of Gadianton’s band, are furious. They urge the people to seize Nephi and have him condemned for a supposed crime.
They accuse him of “reviling,” or verbally attacking, the people and the law.

f.g: To speak abusively against; to insult.

chapters.n: Mormon clarifies: Nephi had exposed how corrupt their laws had become, but nothing he said went against God’s commandments. Much of his speech was not recorded.
The judges are angry because Nephi named their secret crimes plainly. Yet they dare not touch him themselves, fearing the crowd would turn on them.
So they work on the crowd: Why let this man insult us? He predicts our destruction and the loss of our great cities.

f.g: Allow or permit.

chapters.n: Their boast: we are powerful and our cities great, so no enemy can touch us. Pride in their own strength is the very sin Nephi warned about.
The crowd divides. Some defend Nephi as a good man whose warnings will come true unless they repent.
These defenders admit that Nephi correctly described their many sins, so he surely knows their future just as well.
They conclude he must be a prophet, for no one else could know these things.
Fearing the crowd, Nephi’s enemies hold back. Seeing that some now favor him, Nephi speaks again.
Nephi reminds them of Moses, whom God empowered to part the Red Sea so Israel crossed on dry ground while the Egyptian army drowned.

f.g: This way and that; to either side.

chapters.n: If God gave Moses such power, why do they doubt that He could give Nephi knowledge of coming judgments?
They deny not only Nephi’s words but also those of all their ancestors, including Moses, who prophesied of the Messiah.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ, “anointed one”; Greek Christos.

chapters.n: Moses testified of the Son of God. Just as Moses lifted up a bronze serpent in the wilderness, Christ would be “lifted up” on the cross.
Whoever looked at the serpent lived; likewise, whoever looks to the Son of God with faith and a contrite spirit can receive eternal life. Salvation is as simple as looking to Christ.

f.g: A humble, repentant heart.

chapters.n: Moses was not alone. All the holy prophets testified of Christ, reaching back to the time of Abraham.
Abraham himself saw Christ’s coming and rejoiced, as Jesus later said.
Even before Abraham, many were ordained after the order of the Son of God, the holy priesthood, so people thousands of years earlier could know redemption would come.

f.w: after the order of his Son

chapters.n: After Abraham, many prophets testified of Christ. Zenos, a prophet of Israel known from the brass plates, testified so boldly that he was killed for it.

f.g: An Israelite prophet quoted from the brass plates but absent from the Bible.

chapters.n: Nephi lists more witnesses: Zenock, Ezias, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Jeremiah foretold Jerusalem’s destruction, and it happened. So why doubt his prophecy of the Son of God?

f.g: A prophet otherwise unknown; mentioned only here.

chapters.n: Living proof is among them: King Zedekiah’s sons were killed except Mulek, and Mulek’s descendants, the people of Zarahemla, live with the Nephites.

f.w: the sons of Zedekiah were not slain

chapters.n: Lehi was driven from Jerusalem for testifying of Christ. Nephi and nearly all their forefathers since have looked forward to Christ’s day with joy.
Christ is God. He was with these ancient prophets, revealed Himself to them, and redeemed them, even before His birth. They praised Him for what He would do.
Since they cannot honestly deny these evidences, rejecting them is sin. Everything in heaven and earth testifies that these things are true.

f.w: all things which are in the earth, as a witness

chapters.n: They have rebelled against God. Instead of storing treasure in heaven, where nothing decays, they are storing up wrath for judgment day.
Because of murder, sexual sin, and wickedness, they are ripening for destruction, and unless they repent it will come soon.
Then Nephi delivers a startling sign: go to the judgment-seat and you will find the chief judge murdered in his own blood, killed by his own brother who wants his seat.

f.w: it is now even at your doors

chapters.n: Both the victim and his murderer belong to the secret band founded by Gadianton and ultimately by Satan, who seeks to destroy souls.

f.w: the evil one who seeketh to destroy the souls of men

chapters.n: As soon as Nephi finishes, five men from the crowd run to the judgment-seat to test his claim, talking among themselves as they go.
They are skeptics, but fair-minded ones: if the judge is really dead, they will accept that Nephi’s other words are true as well. They put the prophecy to an honest test.

f.g: For certain.

f.w: if this thing which he has said

chapters.n: Running as fast as they can, they find the chief judge lying dead in his blood, exactly as Nephi said.
Stunned, they collapse to the ground. They had not truly believed Nephi.
Now they believe, and they tremble with fear that all of Nephi’s predicted judgments will also come true.
Mormon backtracks: right after the murder, committed in secret by the judge’s brother, the servants raised the alarm.

f.g: A disguise or cover of secrecy.

chapters.n: People rush to the judgment-seat and are startled to find five men lying on the ground.
Knowing nothing of the scene at Nephi’s garden, they assume these five are the murderers, struck down by God so they could not escape.
The five are tied up and jailed, and word goes out that the killers have been caught. It is a dramatic case of mistaken identity.

f.g: A public announcement spread throughout the land.

chapters.n: The next day the people gather to mourn and fast at the chief judge’s burial.
The judges who had heard Nephi in his garden also attend.
They ask where the five messengers are. The people reply that they know of no messengers, only five murderers now in prison.
When the prisoners are brought out, they are the five messengers. They explain everything.
They found everything as Nephi said, fell down in shock, and were jailed when they came to.
They don’t know who the killer is; they only know the judge was dead, just as Nephi foretold.
The corrupt judges spin the story: Nephi must have hired someone to kill the judge so he could “predict” it, win converts, and make himself look like a great prophet.

f.g: Explain or interpret, here in a twisted way.

chapters.n: They vow to expose Nephi and force him to confess and name the real killer.

f.g: Expose or uncover.

chapters.n: The five are released on burial day. They argue with the judges one by one and refute their accusations against Nephi.

f.g: Leave confused and unable to answer.

chapters.n: Still, the judges have Nephi arrested and brought before the crowd, questioning him in many ways to trap him into a capital charge.

f.g: Various; many different.
Trip him up in contradictions.

chapters.n: They accuse him of being an accomplice and offer him money and his life if he names the murderer and admits to the plot. The bribe reveals their own corruption.

f.g: An accomplice; a partner in a plot.

chapters.n: Nephi’s reply is blunt: fools, uncircumcised in heart, blind and stubborn. How long do you think the Lord will put up with your sin?

f.g: Outwardly part of the covenant people but inwardly unchanged.
Tolerate; allow.

chapters.n: They should be weeping and mourning over the destruction coming unless they repent.

f.g: Wail loudly in grief.

chapters.n: Nephi explains that he revealed the murder only as a witness that he knows their hidden wickedness. Here we learn the judge’s name, Seezoram.

f.g: The murdered chief judge; mentioned only in this chapter.

chapters.n: Because he gave them a sign, they are angry and want to kill him, a response the scriptures often predict for those who demand signs.
So Nephi offers a second sign to see if they will still try to kill him.
Go to the house of Seantum, Seezoram’s brother.

f.g: The judge’s brother and murderer; mentioned only here.

chapters.n: Ask him whether Nephi, “the pretended prophet,” conspired with him to murder his brother. Nephi even scripts their mocking words.

f.g: A supposed or false prophet; Nephi quotes his critics’ own label.

chapters.n: Nephi predicts Seantum will answer no.
Then ask him directly whether he murdered his brother.
Seantum will be afraid and not know what to say. He will deny it and act surprised, claiming innocence.

f.g: Knew not.

chapters.n: But examine him and you will find blood on the hem of his cloak.

f.g: The lower edges or hem of a garment.

chapters.n: Ask him where the blood came from: is it not your brother’s?
He will tremble and go deathly pale.
Point out that his fear and pallor show his guilt.
Then, overcome with fear, he will confess and stop denying the murder.
He will also say that Nephi knew nothing except what God revealed. Then they will know Nephi is honest and sent from God.
Everything happens exactly as Nephi said: first denial, then confession.
Seantum is proven to be the murderer. The five and Nephi are all set free.
Some believe Nephi’s words; others believe through the five, who had been converted while in prison.
Some now say Nephi is a prophet.
Others go too far and call him a god, since he knew their hearts and exposed the murderer. Yet as the next chapter shows, many others simply walk away unchanged.
Despite the miracle, the crowd splits up and drifts away, each going their own way and leaving Nephi standing alone.

f.g: In various directions.

chapters.n: Nephi walks home, pondering what the Lord had shown him. Pondering, thinking deeply about sacred things, often comes right before revelation in scripture.
He is discouraged by the people’s secret crimes, murders, and wickedness. While he is pondering in this low moment, the Lord’s voice comes to him.

f.g: Discouraged; downhearted.

chapters.n: The Lord blesses Nephi for preaching tirelessly, without fear, not seeking to save his own life but seeking God’s will. God noticed his faithfulness even when no one else listened.

f.g: Tireless, persistent effort.

f.w: hast not sought thine own life

chapters.n: Because of this, the Lord will make Nephi mighty in word, deed, faith, and works. Whatever Nephi asks will be done, because Nephi will never ask against God’s will. His power rests on complete trust.

f.w: thou shalt not ask that which is contrary to my will

chapters.n: “Thou art Nephi, and I am God.” Before His angels, the Lord gives Nephi power to send famine, plague, and destruction according to the people’s wickedness.

f.w: in the presence of mine angels

chapters.n: The Lord gives Nephi the sealing power: what he binds or seals on earth will be bound in heaven. Jesus gave the same power to Peter, and Latter-day Saints believe it was restored through Elijah in 1836.

f.w: whatsoever ye shall seal on earth shall be sealed in heaven

chapters.n: With this power, if Nephi said a temple would be torn apart, it would happen.

f.g: Torn in two.

chapters.n: Even mountains would obey him and be leveled, echoing Jesus’s teaching about faith moving mountains.
If Nephi declared that God would strike the people, it would come to pass.
Then the Lord gives a command: go and warn the people that unless they repent, they will be destroyed. The power comes with a mission.

f.g: A title meaning all-powerful.

chapters.n: Nephi does not even finish going home. He turns around at once and goes back to the scattered crowds to deliver the Lord’s warning. His obedience is immediate.

f.w: did not go unto his own house

chapters.n: Even after the miracle about the chief judge, the people harden their hearts and refuse to listen.
Nephi delivers the message plainly: repent or be destroyed.
They still refuse, insult him, and try to arrest him.

f.g: Speak abusively against.

chapters.n: But God’s power protects him. The Spirit carries him away from among them so they cannot seize him.
By the Spirit, Nephi goes from crowd to crowd until everyone has heard God’s word, directly or through his messengers.
They still won’t listen. Contention grows until they turn on each other with the sword, a civil war.
So ends the seventy-first year of the judges, about 21 BC.
In the seventy-second year (about 20 BC), contention becomes open war throughout the Nephite lands.
The Gadianton band is behind this destruction, and the war drags on for two full years.
Nephi now uses the power God gave him, but in prayer.

He asks God not to let the people be destroyed by the sword, but to send famine instead, hoping hunger will make them remember God and repent. It is a merciful request: famine humbles, war only destroys.
God does what Nephi asks. A great famine comes. Death by the sword stops, but death by hunger becomes severe.

f.g: Severe; grievous.

chapters.n: The drought continues into the next year. Crops fail across the land, among Lamanites and Nephites alike, and thousands die, especially in the more wicked regions.
Facing starvation, the people finally remember the Lord and recall Nephi’s words.
They beg their leaders to ask Nephi, whom they now call a man of God, to pray the famine away before his prophecies of destruction come true.
When Nephi sees that they have truly repented and humbled themselves in sackcloth, he prays again.

f.g: Coarse cloth worn as a sign of mourning and repentance.

chapters.n: Nephi reports their repentance: they have wiped out the Gadianton band and buried its secret plans in the earth.

f.w: concealed their secret plans in the earth
f.g: They hid the band’s written oaths and plans so they could not be used again.

chapters.n: He asks God to let His anger be satisfied by the destruction of the wicked men already gone, and to spare the humbled survivors.

f.g: Satisfied; calmed.

chapters.n: He pleads for the Lord to turn away His fierce anger and end the famine.
He asks for rain so the earth can bring forth fruit and grain in their seasons.
Nephi prays with confidence: God heard him before when he asked for famine, and God promised to spare the people if they repented.

f.g: The plague of war.

f.w: If this people repent I will spare them

chapters.n: And Nephi points out that they have repented, humbled by famine and destruction.
He asks God to “try again”: give them another chance to see whether they will serve Him, and bless them as promised. It reflects God’s patience across the Nephite pride cycle.

f.g: Test them once more.

chapters.n: In the seventy-sixth year the Lord answers. Rain falls, and the earth again yields fruit and grain in their seasons.

f.w: rain should fall upon the earth

chapters.n: The people rejoice and praise God. They no longer try to kill Nephi but honor him as a great prophet with power from God.

f.g: Regard highly; respect.

chapters.n: His brother Lehi was just as righteous.

f.g: Not the least bit behind; fully equal.

chapters.n: The Nephites prosper again, rebuild ruined places, and spread across the land from sea to sea, north and south.

f.g: Ruined or abandoned areas.

f.w: from the sea west to the sea east

chapters.n: Peace continues through the next year. The church spreads, and most Nephites and Lamanites belong to it.
The seventy-eighth year is also peaceful, apart from a few disagreements about doctrines the prophets had taught.
Strife grows the next year, but Nephi, Lehi, and others who understood true doctrine and received daily revelation end it within the year through preaching.
In the eightieth year (about 12 BC), Nephite dissenters who had joined the Lamanites, along with some true Lamanites they stirred up, start a war.
They raid, kill, and plunder, then retreat to hiding places in the mountains and wilderness, growing daily as more dissenters join them. This is guerrilla warfare.
Within a few years they become a huge band. They dig up Gadianton’s old secret plans and become Gadianton robbers again. The buried evil returns.

f.w: search out all the secret plans of Gadianton

chapters.n: These robbers cause great havoc among both Nephites and Lamanites.

f.g: Widespread destruction.

chapters.n: To stop them, an army of strong men is sent into the wilderness and mountains to hunt them down.
But that same year the army is pushed back to its own lands. The eightieth year ends.
At the start of the eighty-first year they attack again, killing many robbers but suffering heavy losses themselves.
Again they must retreat, because the robbers in the mountains and wilderness are too many.

f.g: Overran in large numbers, like a plague.

chapters.n: The robbers keep growing, strong enough to defy both Nephite and Lamanite armies, and the whole land lives in fear.
They raid widely, killing many and carrying off captives, especially women and children, into the wilderness.
This suffering, brought on by the people’s sins, again stirs them to remember God.
The eighty-first year ends.
Then, year by year, the slide begins again: forgetting God, growing in sin, refusing to change. Mormon tracks the decline one year at a time.

f.g: Improve; correct.

chapters.n: By the eighty-fifth year, pride and wickedness are growing stronger, and they are ripening again for destruction.
The eighty-fifth year ends, about 7 BC. The next chapter is Mormon’s reflection on why people keep repeating this cycle.
Mormon steps back from the story to teach. Human hearts are unreliable and unsteady, yet the Lord, in His endless goodness, blesses and prospers those who trust Him.

f.g: Mormon’s signal that he is drawing a lesson from the history.
Fickleness; quickness to change.

chapters.n: The tragic irony: right when God is blessing His people most, with crops, wealth, safety, and peace, they harden their hearts and forget Him. Ease and prosperity, not hardship, are what lead them away.

f.g: A title for God, here for Jesus Christ.

chapters.n: So unless the Lord disciplines them with trials, even death, terror, and famine, they won’t remember Him. Mormon sees affliction as a form of God’s love.

f.g: Correct or discipline, with the aim of improving.

chapters.n: Mormon laments how foolish and evil people can be: quick to sin, slow to do good, quick to listen to the devil and chase empty things.
They are quick to become proud and boast, and slow to remember God, listen to His counsel, or walk in wisdom’s paths.
The root problem: people don’t want their Creator to rule over them. Despite His kindness, they ignore His counsel and refuse His guidance.

f.g: Treat as worthless; disregard.

chapters.n: Mormon says people are “less than the dust of the earth.” This isn’t a statement of human worth to God but a comparison of obedience, as the next verse explains.

f.w: less than the dust of the earth

chapters.n: Even dust obeys God, moving wherever He commands. People, with agency, often don’t.

f.g: Separating apart.

chapters.n: At God’s voice hills and mountains tremble.

f.w: the hills and the mountains tremble

chapters.n: His voice can break mountains down and level them like a valley.
By His voice the entire earth shakes.
Even the earth’s deep foundations rock at His word.
When He tells the earth to move, it moves.
If He tells the earth to “go back” and lengthen the day, it happens, a likely reference to Joshua’s long day.
Mormon adds a striking note: it only looks as though the sun stands still; in fact, it is the earth that moves. His remark fits what we now know about the earth’s rotation.

f.w: it is the earth that moveth and not the sun
f.g: Mormon wrote this about AD 380, over a thousand years before Copernicus.

chapters.n: If He commands the ocean depths to dry up, they do, as at the Red Sea.

f.w: the waters of the great deep

chapters.n: He can lift a mountain and drop it on a city, a detail that came true at Christ’s death when the city of Moronihah was buried.
If a wicked person hides treasure and God curses it, it is cursed. This anticipates Samuel’s prophecy about “slippery” treasures.

f.w: hide up a treasure in the earth

chapters.n: If God says the treasure will never be found, no one will ever find it.
Likewise, if the Lord pronounces a person cursed because of sin, it happens.
And if He says a person will be cut off from His presence because of sin, He makes it so.
Woe to anyone who keeps sinning and so cannot be saved. That is exactly why God has proclaimed repentance: so people can be saved.
Blessed are those who repent and listen to the Lord. They are the ones who will be saved.
Mormon prays that God will bring people to repentance and good works, so they may be “restored unto grace for grace,” receiving more of God’s grace as they live by it.
Mormon wishes everyone could be saved, but scripture says some will be cast out of the Lord’s presence at the last day.

f.w: I would that all men might be saved

chapters.n: They will be consigned to misery, fulfilling the words that the good receive everlasting life and the evil everlasting damnation. Mormon ends his sermon with a solemn “Amen.”

f.w: They that have done good shall have everlasting life

f.g: Being stopped or condemned; unable to progress into God’s presence.

chapters.n: In the eighty-sixth year (about 6 BC), the Nephites remain deeply wicked, while the Lamanites strictly obey God, keeping the law of Moses as they awaited Christ.

f.w: according to the law of Moses

chapters.n: A Lamanite named Samuel comes to Zarahemla and preaches repentance for many days. The Nephites throw him out, and he starts home.
The Lord tells him to go back and say whatever the Lord puts into his heart.

Barred from the city, Samuel climbs onto the city wall, stretches out his hand, and shouts the prophecy the Lord gives him. The image of the prophet on the wall is one of the Book of Mormon’s most memorable.
Samuel identifies himself and his message: the sword of justice hangs over this people, and within 400 years it will fall. The Nephites were destroyed about AD 385, fulfilling it.
Only repentance and faith in Jesus Christ can save them. Christ will surely come into the world, suffer much, and be killed for His people.

f.w: shall be slain for his people

chapters.n: An angel brought Samuel this good news, and he came to share it, but they refused him. The gospel is “glad tidings” even when delivered as a warning.
Because of their hard hearts, the Lord will take away His word and Spirit unless they repent, and will turn the Lamanites against them.
Within 400 years they will be struck by war, famine, and disease.

f.g: Deadly disease or plague.

chapters.n: Some of the fourth generation of their enemies will live to see their total destruction. Latter-day Saints often connect the “fourth generation” with the generations after Christ’s visit.
But if they repent, the Lord will turn away His anger. Blessed are the repentant; woe to the unrepentant. Judgment is never inevitable for those who turn back.
Zarahemla is preserved only because of the righteous in it, yet most of its people will harden their hearts.

f.w: because of those who are righteous

chapters.n: The repentant will be spared. Without the righteous, the Lord would send fire from heaven, as on Sodom.

f.w: fire should come down out of heaven

chapters.n: The city survives for the righteous’ sake, but when they cast out the righteous, they will be ripe for destruction. This is exactly what happens before Christ’s death.

f.w: when ye shall cast out the righteous

chapters.n: Woe also to the city of Gideon for its wickedness.
And woe to every Nephite city around them.
A curse will come on the land itself because of the people’s wickedness. “Lord of Hosts” means Lord of armies, both heavenly and earthly.

f.g: A title of God as commander of heaven’s armies.

chapters.n: Anyone who buries treasure will lose it because of the curse, unless he is righteous and hides it “unto the Lord.” In a world without banks, burying valuables was common.

f.w: hide up treasures in the earth

chapters.n: The Lord wants people to “hide up their treasures” to Him, dedicating their wealth to God. Only the righteous do, and wealth kept selfishly is cursed and lost.

f.w: hide up their treasures unto me

chapters.n: A day will come when, fleeing enemies, they bury their wealth because their hearts are on it. Since they won’t dedicate it to God, both they and their treasure will be cursed.
The people are cursed because of their riches, and their riches are cursed, because they have set their hearts on wealth and ignored the One who gave it.
They never thank God for their blessings but always remember their riches. Their hearts swell with pride, envy, strife, malice, persecution, and murder.
That is why God has cursed the land and their riches.
Woe to them for casting out, mocking, stoning, and killing prophets, just as their ancestors did. Israel had a long history of rejecting prophets.
They claim that if they had lived in their fathers’ day, they would never have killed the prophets.

f.w: we would not have slain the prophets

chapters.n: Samuel says they are worse: when a prophet points out their sins, they get angry, call him false, a sinner, and of the devil, and try to destroy him.
But if someone says, “Do whatever you like, there’s no sin in it, follow your own pride,” they welcome him as a prophet.

f.w: Walk after the pride of your own hearts

chapters.n: They lavish gold, silver, and fine clothes on such a man, because he flatters them and says “all is well.”

f.g: Possessions; wealth.

chapters.n: Samuel cries out: wicked and perverse generation, how long will you follow blind guides and choose darkness over light?
The Lord’s anger is already kindled, and He has cursed the land.

f.g: Set on fire; aroused.

chapters.n: Their riches will become “slippery,” impossible to hold onto, and in their poverty they won’t be able to keep anything.
In their poverty they will cry to the Lord in vain, because their destruction will already be sealed. They will weep and howl and lament.
Their lament: if only we had repented and not killed the prophets; if only we had remembered God when He gave us riches, they would not have slipped away.
A tool set down disappears overnight; swords vanish just when needed for battle. The land’s curse makes nothing secure.
Buried treasures slip away because of the curse.
If only they had repented when the Lord’s word came. Now everything is slippery and cannot be held.
They will feel surrounded by demons, the angels of the destroyer, confessing great sins and asking whether God can turn away His anger. This will be their language then.

f.w: the angels of him who hath sought to destroy our souls

chapters.n: But their probation will be over. They put off salvation until it was forever too late, searching all their lives for happiness in sin, which is impossible because it goes against God’s righteous nature.

f.w: procrastinated the day of your salvation

f.g: The time given in mortal life to prepare to meet God.

chapters.n: Samuel ends with a plea and a prayer: that they would hear, that God’s anger would turn away, and that they would repent and be saved. His harsh warning comes from love.
Mormon notes that Samuel prophesied much more than could be recorded.
Samuel gives a dated sign: in five more years the Son of God will come to redeem all who believe on His name. The count matters, as the believers later wait anxiously for this deadline.
The first sign of Christ’s birth: great lights in the heavens, so that the night before His coming will have no darkness and will seem like day.
People will see the sun set and rise as usual, yet the night between will stay bright, so it will seem like one long day. This will be the night before His birth.

f.w: one day and a night and a day

chapters.n: A new star will appear, unlike any they have seen, another sign, matching the star the wise men followed in the Old World.
There will also be many other signs and wonders in the sky.
People will be so amazed that they fall to the ground.
The point of the signs: whoever believes on the Son of God will have everlasting life.

f.w: whosoever shall believe on the Son of God

chapters.n: An angel commanded Samuel to deliver this message: “repent and prepare the way of the Lord,” the same call later given to John the Baptist.

f.w: prepare the way of the Lord

chapters.n: Samuel names their real objections: he is a Lamanite, and his words were hard to hear. So they are angry, want to kill him, and have thrown him out.
That is why he stands on the wall: so they cannot avoid hearing about God’s coming judgments and the conditions on which they can repent.
He also wants them to know of the coming of Jesus Christ, whom he calls the Father of heaven and earth and Creator of all things, and of the signs of His coming, so they will believe.

f.w: the Father of heaven and of earth

chapters.n: True belief in His name leads to repentance and forgiveness of sins through His merits, His goodness and sacrifice rather than our own.

f.g: Forgiveness; release from the debt of sin.

chapters.n: Next Samuel gives a sign of Christ’s death.
Christ must die for salvation to come. His death makes the resurrection possible, so that all people can be brought back into the Lord’s presence.

f.g: Is necessary or fitting.

chapters.n: Through the Fall, all humanity was cut off from God’s presence, counted as dead both physically and spiritually. Christ’s death and resurrection redeem everyone from that first spiritual death.

f.g: Here, the separation from God that came to all through Adam’s fall.

chapters.n: Christ’s resurrection redeems all mankind and brings everyone back into the Lord’s presence, at least for judgment.

f.w: bringeth them back into the presence of the Lord

chapters.n: It also makes repentance possible. The repentant escape being “hewn down”; the unrepentant suffer a second spiritual death, cut off again from what pertains to righteousness.

f.w: hewn down and cast into the fire

chapters.n: So repent, Samuel urges. Knowing these truths and not acting on them brings condemnation and the second death.

f.w: knowing these things and not doing them

chapters.n: The sign of His death: the sun, moon, and stars will go dark, with no light in the land for three days, from His death until His resurrection.

f.w: for the space of three days

chapters.n: When He dies there will be hours of thunder and lightning, the earth will quake, and the solid rock, above and below ground, will be shattered.

f.g: Die; give up one’s spirit.

chapters.n: The rocks will be split and forever after show seams, cracks, and broken fragments across the earth.
Great storms will come; mountains will sink into valleys and valleys rise into high mountains.

f.g: Violent storms.

chapters.n: Highways will break apart and many cities will be left in ruins.
Many graves will open and saints will appear to many people, just as happened in Jerusalem after Jesus rose.
Samuel stresses that an angel told him these things, including hours of thunder and lightning.
The angel also said darkness would cover the whole earth for three days while these things happened.
Many will see even greater things, so that no one will have reason to disbelieve. God gives abundant evidence.
The purpose: whoever believes can be saved, and whoever refuses will face a just judgment. The condemned bring condemnation on themselves.

f.w: bring upon themselves their own condemnation

chapters.n: A great statement on agency. Whoever perishes or sins does it to himself, because God has given knowledge and made people free to act for themselves.
God gave people the ability to know good from evil and to choose life or death. Whatever they choose, good or evil, will be restored to them. This is the law of restoration.

f.w: restored unto that which is good

chapters.n: Samuel continues: unless the Nephites repent, their homes will be left empty and ruined. Jesus used the same phrase about Jerusalem.

f.w: your houses shall be left unto you desolate

chapters.n: He describes the suffering of war in human terms: nursing mothers and pregnant women unable to flee, trampled and left to die. It echoes Jesus’s warnings about Jerusalem’s fall.

f.g: Nurse a baby.

f.w: wo unto them which are with child

chapters.n: The Nephites have been the Lord’s chosen people. He loved them, and because He loved them, He corrected them during their times of sin.

f.w: chastened them because he loveth them

chapters.n: By contrast, the Lord “hated” the Lamanites’ evil deeds, which came from false traditions. Yet salvation reached them through Nephite preaching, and for that purpose God prolonged their lives. God’s rejection was of their deeds, not of them as people.

f.g: In Hebrew idiom, often means “rejected” or “loved less,” here tied to their evil deeds.

chapters.n: Most Lamanites are now on the path of duty, living carefully before God and keeping His commandments under the law of Moses.

f.g: Carefully, watchfully, with attention to every step.

chapters.n: They work tirelessly to bring the rest of their people to the truth, and new converts join daily.
The Nephites have seen it themselves: Lamanites who learn the truth and believe the scriptures and prophets are led to faith in the Lord and repentance, which bring a change of heart.
Those who reach this point are firm and steadfast in the faith and in the freedom it gives.
The Nephites also know these converts buried their weapons and would rather be killed than risk sinning by shedding blood. Their faith in Christ shows in their fear of sin.
Because they stay firm once enlightened, the Lord will bless them and prolong their days, despite their failings.
Even if they later fall away in unbelief, the Lord will preserve them until the time foretold by Zenos and other prophets when the Lamanites will be restored to the truth.

f.w: the restoration of our brethren, the Lamanites

chapters.n: In the last days the Lord’s promises extend to the Lamanites. Although they will be driven, hunted, and scattered, the Lord will be merciful to them.
Prophecy says they will again come to know their Redeemer, the true Shepherd, and be counted among His sheep. The Book of Mormon itself was written partly for this purpose.
So, unless the Nephites repent, things will go better for the Lamanites than for them.

f.w: better for them than for you

chapters.n: If the Lamanites had seen the miracles the Nephites have seen, they would never have fallen into unbelief. Greater light brings greater responsibility.

f.w: had the mighty works been shown unto them

chapters.n: So the Lord promises not to destroy the Lamanites completely; in His own time they will return to Him.

f.w: in the day of my wisdom
f.g: At the time God judges best.

chapters.n: But the Nephites, if they won’t repent, will be utterly destroyed for their unbelief despite all God’s mighty works. This came true about four centuries later.
Many who heard Samuel believe. They find Nephi, openly confess their sins, and ask to be baptized. Samuel the Lamanite and Nephi the Nephite work as partners in the same cause.
Unbelievers grow angry and throw stones and shoot arrows at Samuel on the wall. But the Spirit of the Lord protects him, and nothing hits him.
Seeing the miracle, many more believe and go to Nephi for baptism.
Nephi is baptizing, prophesying, preaching repentance, and working miracles so people will know Christ is coming soon.
He tells them of coming events in advance so that, when they happen, people will remember they were foretold and believe.

Most people still don’t believe. Unable to hit Samuel, they tell their captains he has a devil in him and must be seized and bound. They explain away a miracle by blaming the devil, as Jesus’s enemies did.
As they move to grab him, Samuel jumps down from the wall and escapes to his own land, where he keeps preaching among the Lamanites.
The Nephites never hear from him again. Centuries later, though, the risen Jesus asked that Samuel’s prophecies be added to the record.
The eighty-sixth year of the judges ends (about 6 BC).
In the eighty-seventh year most remain proud and wicked; a minority walk carefully before God.

f.g: Carefully and watchfully.

chapters.n: The same conditions continue in the eighty-eighth year.
In the eighty-ninth year little changes, except that people grow even more hardened in sin.

f.g: Change.

chapters.n: In the ninetieth year (about 2 BC), great signs and wonders appear, and the prophets’ words begin to be fulfilled.
Angels appear to wise men and announce “glad tidings of great joy,” the same words the angel spoke to the shepherds near Bethlehem.
Yet most people harden their hearts, except the most believing Nephites and Lamanites, and rely on their own strength and wisdom.
The skeptics’ first argument: the prophets made so many guesses that some were bound to be right, but these great events cannot really happen.
They begin reasoning and arguing among themselves.
Their second argument: it isn’t reasonable that a Christ would come. And if He is the Son of God, why would He show Himself only at Jerusalem and not to them?
Why not show Himself in this land too? Ironically, the risen Christ will do exactly that.
Their third argument: this is just a tradition passed down by their fathers about something far away that no one can verify, used to keep them ignorant.
Their fourth argument: religious leaders use mysterious tricks to keep people dependent on them as servants. It is a cynical view of faith that Korihor once used too.

f.w: keep us down to be servants

chapters.n: People imagined many more foolish ideas. Satan kept them stirred up, spreading rumors and contention everywhere to harden hearts against good and against Christ’s coming.
Despite all the signs, wonders, and miracles among the Lord’s people, Satan gains a strong hold on hearts throughout the land.

f.w: Satan did get great hold upon the hearts

chapters.n: The ninetieth year of the judges ends.
The book of Helaman closes, drawn from the records of Helaman and his sons Nephi and Lehi. The next book, Third Nephi, opens on the eve of Christ’s birth.
